title: Container Lifecycle: Stop, Start, Restart 🔄
description: Take full control of your containers – stop, start, restart, remove, and inspect logs.

slides.title: Stopping a Container Gracefully ✋
slides.content:
# `docker stop`

Sends a **SIGTERM** signal to the main process inside the container. If the process doesn’t stop within a timeout (10s by default), Docker sends a **SIGKILL**.

```bash
docker stop <container-name-or-id>
```

**Example:**
```bash
docker stop my-nginx
```

The container enters the “exited” state (status code 0 if successful).

slides.title: Killing a Container (Force) 💀
slides.content:
# `docker kill`

Sends a **SIGKILL** immediately. No grace period. Use when a container is unresponsive.

```bash
docker kill <container>
```

You can also specify a different signal with `-s`:
```bash
docker kill -s SIGINT my-app
```

quizData.question: What is the main difference between `docker stop` and `docker kill`?

options.text: `stop` deletes the container; `kill` only pauses it.
`stop` sends a SIGTERM (graceful), `kill` sends a SIGKILL (forced).
There is no difference; they are aliases.

quizData.explanation: `stop` tries to gracefully shut down the container, allowing cleanup. `kill` forces an immediate termination.

slides.title: Starting and Restarting Containers 🔁
slides.content:
# `docker start` & `docker restart`

- `docker start <container>` – starts a previously stopped container. It resumes with the same settings and state (unless ephemeral).
- `docker restart <container>` – stops and then starts the container in one command (like a reboot).

**Example:**
```bash
docker start my-nginx
docker restart my-nginx
```

Note: `docker start` does **not** create a new container; it reuses the existing one.

quizData.question: If you have a stopped container named `db`, which command brings it back to life?
quizData.explanation: `docker start` is used to restart an existing stopped container. `docker run` would create a brand new container.

slides.title: Removing Containers Permanently 🗑️
slides.content:
# `docker rm` / `docker container rm`

To delete a container from disk (its writable layer is gone).

```bash
docker rm <container>
```

- You can only remove **stopped** containers (use `-f` to force remove a running one).
- Remove multiple at once: `docker rm con1 con2`
- Remove all stopped containers:
  ```bash
  docker container prune
  ```

> Pro tip: Use `--rm` when you `docker run` to avoid manual cleanup later.

quizData.question: You can remove a running container with `docker rm` without any extra flags.
quizData.explanation: Docker refuses to remove a running container unless you add the `-f` (force) flag. Safest practice: stop first, then remove.

slides.title: Checking Container Logs 📜
slides.content:
# `docker logs`

See what your container printed to stdout/stderr.

```bash
docker logs <container>
```

Useful options:
- `-f` – follow the log in real time (like `tail -f`)
- `--tail N` – show only the last N lines
- `-t` – show timestamps

**Example:**
```bash
docker logs --tail 20 -f my-nginx
```

quizData.question: How can you watch a container’s logs live as they are written?
quizData.explanation: The `-f` (or `--follow`) flag keeps the log stream open, printing new lines as they come.

slides.title: Lifecycle Recap 📋
slides.content:
## Quick Summary

| Action        | Command                     |
|---------------|-----------------------------|
| Create & run  | `docker run`                |
| Stop gracefully| `docker stop`              |
| Force stop    | `docker kill`               |
| Restart       | `docker restart`            |
| Start stopped | `docker start`              |
| Remove        | `docker rm`                 |
| View logs     | `docker logs`               |

Master these and you control any container.
